cards.title: Baseline product-research checklist before any tool
cards.summary: Four pass/fail criteria — margin, problem solved, existing content, shipping weight — that any dropshipping product must clear before deeper research.
cards.use_when: Screening a candidate product or deciding whether a product found via ad spy, Instagram or TikTok is worth further analysis.
steps: Require a gross margin of at least $30–$40 above supplier cost (the source uses this as the margin floor, not a percentage).

Confirm the product solves a clear problem or relieves an insecurity: pain relief, home fitness, hygiene, convenience. Products that only ride a viral trend with no real utility are the ones the source says beginners lose money on.

Check that user-generated content already exists for the product (search TikTok) so you have raw footage for ads and site assets; you can download and re-edit clips, and the source advises against posting someone else's video untouched.
Avoid heavy or oversized items, which create shipping and logistics problems the source calls a nightmare.

Sanity-check that the product is not purely 'junk' from a trend: the source's contrast case is a music projector and a gym-bag product versus a $25 hand massager sold at $80 and a $40 Pilates set sold at $120.
Score each candidate against all four criteria in a Google Sheet alongside buy price, intended sale price and competitor notes before spending on ads.
caveats: The $30–$40 margin figure is the source's rule of thumb for dropshipping, not a universal benchmark; lower-ticket or higher-repeat purchase models may differ.
The source's largest example (a Pilates set bought at $40, sold at $120 with a free guide) is a personal result, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Three fastest ways to fail at product selection
cards.summary: The source's three anti-patterns to avoid: selling what you personally like, copying a competitor as a beginner, and choosing a product with no content online.
cards.use_when: Stress-testing a product idea before committing budget, or diagnosing why previous tests failed.
steps: Do not sell what you personally like — the source says if that worked he'd be selling golf gear and fish pictures. Personal taste is not demand evidence.
Do not take the 'copy a competitor and make it slightly better' route as a beginner; the source calls it the oldest trick in the book and says it does not work for newcomers.
Reject products with no existing online content. Content availability is a hard requirement because you need raw video to build ads and product pages.
Look instead for something untapped: un-niched utility products for beginners, or a saturated product with an unclaimed buyer segment.
Treat the presence of many competitors as a demand signal, not an automatic veto — but only if you have a concrete plan to reach a different audience (see Blue Ocean angle pivoting).
caveats: The source's claim that he now succeeds with roughly one of every two products tested is a personal anecdote, not an expected hit rate.

cards.title: Random, un-niched products as the beginner entry path
cards.summary: For first-time dropshippers the source recommends deliberately random utility products outside mainstream niches to sidestep competition and high ad costs.
cards.use_when: Choosing a first product or first test when you have little experience and no brand equity.
steps: Pick products that belong to no obvious niche — the source's examples are a portable bubble bath (cost ~$40, sell ~$90) and a shoe cleaner/sterilizer that dries shoes in about 30 seconds.
Deliberately skip crowded verticals: no generic dog products, no mass-market beauty aimed at women unless the product itself is new and unique.
Expect to be crushed by competition or pay far more per click in those crowded niches as a beginner.
Verify the candidate still clears the baseline checklist (margin, problem, content, shipping weight) — 'random' means un-niched, not low-quality.
Treat this as the easiest on-ramp, not a permanent rule: the source explicitly says it is 'by no means a must-do' and later shows how to compete in saturated categories.
caveats: The source frames this as a beginner convenience strategy; experienced operators can compete directly and the source moves on to Blue Ocean pivoting for them.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Meta Ad Library method: find dropshippers via generic keywords
cards.summary: Free method that surfaces live dropshipping ads by searching generic offer keywords and filtering to active ads — then cross-checking saturation.
cards.use_when: Starting product research with no paid tools, or validating whether other stores are currently advertising a product.
steps: Open the Meta Ad Library and search generic dropshipping terms such as 'free shipping' or '50% off'; these attract dropshipping stores rather than brand advertisers.
Apply the Active ads filter, and optionally restrict to ads launched in the last one to two weeks to bias toward new tests.

Scroll the results and screen each product against the baseline checklist (margin, problem, content, weight); the source rejects low-margin jewelry but flags an eye-bag/under-eye product bought around $30 and sold at €69 (~$75) as a real candidate.
Take the product name and search it again in the ad library to count distinct stores currently running it.
Proceed if fewer than five stores are running ads on it in the last seven days; fewer than three is the source's even-better signal.
Repeat with vertical keywords like 'pain relief' to surface problem-solving products rather than novelty items.
caveats: Fewer than five active advertisers in the last week is the source's threshold, not a statistical guarantee of success.
Ad Library counts can be noisy; verify the stores are actually distinct and currently active rather than abandoned pages.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: TikTok cross-check for content supply and demand
cards.summary: Use TikTok to confirm there is usable creative for the product and treat TikTok saturation as acceptable as long as Facebook saturation is low.
cards.use_when: After a product passes the ad-library check, to confirm you have ad footage and to gauge relative saturation across platforms.
steps: Search the exact product term on TikTok and assess the volume of usable product videos you could re-edit into your own ads or embed on the product page.
Download clips with a Facebook video downloader or direct save, then mix/remix them into your own edits rather than reposting them untouched.
Do not reject a product solely because TikTok is saturated — the source explicitly says to take TikTok saturation with a grain of salt because it is a different platform from where you advertise.
Weigh what you see on Facebook/your ad platform far more heavily than TikTok volume when deciding whether to proceed.
Note in your research sheet when a product is heavy on TikTok but light on Facebook — the source treats that gap as an untapped signal worth recording.
caveats: The source's guidance to tolerate TikTok saturation assumes you advertise on Meta; the platform weightings change if your channel is different.
Re-using competitor video without substantial re-editing is a rights and brand risk the source acknowledges.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Instagram Reels feed-training method for product discovery
cards.summary: Turn a fresh Instagram account's Reels feed into a stream of live dropshipping ads by seeding the algorithm with likes on physical-product videos.
cards.use_when: Daily passive product hunting, especially when you want product ideas to come to you rather than searching manually.
steps: Create a brand-new Instagram account so your existing feed data does not pollute the recommendations.
Go to search and look up #winningproduct, then like anywhere from five to ten videos that clearly show physical products, including obvious dropshipping ads.
Return to the Reels tab (the source says this works even better on the mobile app) so the algorithm starts serving dropshipping product ads.
Keep double-tapping every video that fits your criteria — high margin, solves a problem, usable visuals — to reinforce the signal.
Expect a mix of junk; ignore plastic no-value trend items and keep liking only qualifying products.
For each promising product, check AliExpress for the sourcing price (example given: a period-cramp belt bought at $17 and sold at $59), then log it in your research sheet.
Repeat over multiple sessions; the source claims three to five serious candidates within about 30 minutes once the feed is trained.
caveats: The 'three to five winners in 30 minutes' figure is the presenter's own experience and depends on feed quality and country.
Feed training keeps drifting, so keep curating likes rather than assuming the feed stays on-topic.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Winning Hunter paid research: drop-ship filter and competitor thresholds
cards.summary: Use a paid ad-spy tool's dropship filter and AI competitor search to shortlist products, then apply explicit store-count thresholds before testing.
cards.use_when: When you want one tool to surface dropshipping ads and count competitors, and can afford a subscription.
steps: In the tool, select the dropship-ads filter so results only show dropshipping creatives, then scroll and skip obviously irrelevant categories (the source personally avoids the kitchen niche).
Screen candidates against the baseline checklist; the source's worked example is a toothbrush sterilizer that kills bacteria — high margin, clears a real hygiene problem.
Save the ads you like; the source recommends scrolling 10–20 minutes a day to build a saved list, then choosing favourites from it.
Open the competitor's store from the saved ad to judge quality — a store with an awful site is beatable.
Use the tool's AI/competitor search (here 'Magic AI' with a query like 'toothbrush cleaner') to see every store running that product and related products in the category.

Apply the thresholds: proceed only if fewer than about 10 total stores sell it and no more than three are serious competitors (well-built, branded storefronts); a store that is no longer running the product does not count against you.
Treat a clean count as a green flag, then gather video and photo inspiration from the weaker competitor sites to build your own assets.
caveats: Tool names, filters and AI features change — verify the current interface before relying on these exact clicks.
The under-10-stores / max-3-serious-competitors thresholds are the source's heuristics, not validated benchmarks.
The source discloses a discount code but states the tool did not sponsor the video.

cards.title: Daily research log and 3-to-1-to-1 selection funnel
cards.summary: Keep a Google Sheet of candidates with buy price, intended sell price and competitor notes, then narrow three products to one test per day.
cards.use_when: Setting up a repeatable daily product-research routine and deciding what to actually launch.
steps: Create a Google Sheet for researched products and record: product name, buy price, intended sell price, competitor pages to revisit, and free-text notes (e.g. 'seen little on Facebook but heavy on TikTok — untapped').
Add roughly three products per day that pass the baseline criteria.
Narrow those three down to your three favourites — meaning the ones with the strongest margin, clearest problem and weakest competition.
Pick one of the three to actually run as the day's test.
Use the sheet as the working document in reviews or coaching calls so decisions and rationale stay visible.
Revisit competitor pages logged earlier when you need creative or pricing references.
caveats: The source presents this as the routine he reviews with students; it assumes you are running one test at a time and can afford to discard two candidates daily.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Blue Ocean logic: saturated means demand, not dead
cards.summary: Saturation proves demand exists; the opportunity is to serve the same product to an audience nobody is targeting rather than to find a brand-new product.
cards.use_when: When your best-margin candidates all look crowded and you are tempted to abandon them or compete head-on.
steps: Reframe saturation as the presence of proven demand — people already want the product, which removes the risk of teaching the market from scratch.
Instead of competing for the same buyer, hunt for an untargeted sub-demographic or an untargeted geographic market.
Do not try to reinvent the wheel: the source's rule is that you only need to do something nobody else is doing with an otherwise proven product.
Accept a smaller market if you can own it — the source's fishing analogy contrasts three boats fighting over a $20M market with one boat alone on a $2M market.
Treat the second half of product research as thinking about audience, not tooling: the source attributes roughly 50% of the game to finding products and 50% to how you think about marketing them.
caveats: The '100% success rate' claim for geo-arbitrage into untapped European markets is the presenter's assertion, not measured evidence — smaller or unproven markets carry their own risk.
Blue Ocean repositioning only works when the product genuinely suits the new audience; forcing an ill-fitting avatar wastes budget.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Geo-arbitrage: move proven US/UK products into untapped markets
cards.summary: Take a product already validated by US or UK advertising volume and run it in a market where it has not yet been shown.
cards.use_when: You have a proven product with strong English-language ad evidence and want lower competition than the source market.
steps: Identify products with heavy existing US/UK ad volume as proof of demand, not as a place to compete.
Choose a market where the same product has not been advertised (the source cites untapped European countries as his example).
Assume consumer preferences transfer reasonably across similar markets — the source argues people 'like the same products' but simply have not been shown them.
Localise creative and copy to the target market's language and context before launching.
Verify local shipping costs, delivery times and import duties, since these can erase the margin advantage of lower competition.
caveats: The source's confidence in cross-market preference transfer is an opinion; the 'pretty much 100% success rate' phrasing is a claim, not a benchmark.
Logistics, VAT/import rules and payment availability vary by country and must be checked before committing.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Angle pivoting: rebuild a saturated product around a new avatar
cards.summary: Keep the product, change the buyer: identify subsets of customers nobody is targeting and build the whole message around their specific situation.
cards.use_when: When a product is validated but competing ads all speak to one generic audience, and you need a differentiated campaign.
steps: Search the product on TikTok and catalogue the audiences current advertisers target — the source's shoe-dryer example shows everyone selling it generically, with one advertiser targeting football parents.
List alternative avatars the product genuinely serves; for the shoe dryer: parents of kids who get shoes dirty, campers and outdoor enthusiasts with wet gear, and fitness players with smelly shoes.

For a home-fitness product, note that almost all advertisers target young women doing short workouts; the source's untapped angles are older people with stiff joints who won't commit to a gym, and slightly overweight buyers trying to regain control of their life.
Write the ad hook and landing copy around the new avatar's specific pain and desired outcome rather than the product's generic function.
Check that the chosen avatar is a small share of existing advertiser spend (the source cites about 10% for the weight-loss angle) — low share plus real need is the signal.
Keep the product and offer otherwise unchanged so the pivot is a positioning change, not a new sourcing project.
caveats: Visual examples in the source are specific to shoe dryers and home-fitness equipment; the technique generalises but the avatars do not.
Older or lower-tech audiences can require different creative formats and checkout assumptions than the platforms' default dropshipping audience.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Verify blue oceans by auditing what competitors are not doing
cards.summary: A two-step routine: find a problem-solving product, then audit competitor ads to locate the audience or angle none of them occupy.
cards.use_when: Systematically generating differentiated angles for any saturated product you are considering.
steps: Step one: confirm the product solves a real problem and clears the baseline margin, content and shipping criteria.

Step two: research the product's competitors — collect their ads, landing pages and targeting signals, then write down explicitly what they are not doing: which customer type, life circumstance or outcome they never mention.
Look for angles that are visibly rare in the ad set rather than completely absent, since a small amount of validation reduces the risk of an angle nobody wants.
Position your whole campaign on the gap — avatar, hook, imagery, proof — rather than adding it as a secondary message.
Repeat the audit whenever entering a new category; the source frames this as thinking rather than automating, and argues most dropshippers do not do it.
caveats: 'Do something nobody's doing' is the source's maxim and a direction of travel, not evidence that any untaken angle will convert.
Competitor ad libraries only show what is currently running, so recently paused tests can be invisible.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: Judging product quality: real value versus viral junk
cards.summary: Distinguish products that solve a durable human problem and hold margin from cheap trend items that rely on novelty and have no utility.
cards.use_when: Rejecting candidates during any research method, or deciding whether a trending item deserves a test.
steps: Ask whether the product changes the customer's day-to-day life: relieving pain, enabling home workouts, improving hygiene. The source's contrast is a $25 hand massager sold at $80 for daily pain relief versus a music-projector vibe product.
Check the margin math, not the trend: the source rejects products that are cheap with no room for a $30–$40+ markup.
Be sceptical of products whose appeal is purely the trend itself — the source says these come and go and have no real usage.
Remember that passing this filter is necessary but not sufficient: the source notes that even genuinely good products in crowded niches will fail without a differentiation plan.
Use this test during Reels and ad-library scrolling to keep the feed trained on higher-quality candidates.
caveats: Value judgements about what 'helps people' come from the presenter and are subjective; some novelty products do sustain profitable campaigns.
The source's own Pilates and hand-massager examples are his successes and should not be read as typical outcomes.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx

cards.title: What a trained Instagram Reels feed yields and how to read it
cards.summary: Practical expectations for the Reels method: a mix of junk and winners, and a qualification step on AliExpress before logging a product.
cards.use_when: Running the Reels discovery loop and deciding which of the surfaced products to keep.
steps: Expect roughly three categories in the feed: no-value plastic trend junk (discard), quirky but plausible problem solvers (evaluate), and high-value life-improving products (prioritise).
When a plausible product appears — for example a lower-back pain device or a travel suitcase organiser — reinforce it with a like so the feed serves more of that type.
Take the product to AliExpress to establish the real sourcing cost: the source's example is a period-cramp belt at $17 sourced and priced at $59 on the store.
Confirm the margin, the problem solved and that the ad footage is usable before adding it to your sheet.
Keep scrolling in short sessions rather than long ones; the source frames this as something you do continuously, even idly, rather than as a single research block.
caveats: The period-belt pricing is one observed example; sourcing prices and viable retail prices vary by product and market.
Discarding 'junk' too aggressively can filter out categories your audience actually buys, so keep a written rationale rather than gut feel alone.
cards.source_name: Full Product Research Course for Dropshipping (Find Winning Products FAST).docx
